question: What is the difference between a bi-encoder and a cross-encoder?
pos_doc: A bi-encoder embeds queries and candidate documents into dense vectors independently, enabling fast sub-millisecond approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) retrieval over large corpora. In contrast, a cross-encoder performs joint full cross-attention over concatenated query-document pairs, providing richer interaction at the expense of higher O(N) computational cost during inference.
neg_doc: A cross-encoder compresses both query and passage into separate fixed-size dense embeddings that are matched using fast dot-product similarity searches, whereas a bi-encoder runs cross-attention over all pairs jointly.

question: How does contrastive InfoNCE loss train text embedding models?
pos_doc: Contrastive InfoNCE loss optimizes embedding representations by pulling the representations of semantically related query-document pairs closer together in vector space while pushing negative candidates away, scaling similarities by an inverse temperature parameter to sharpen prediction logits.
neg_doc: InfoNCE loss optimizes next-token prediction by computing cross-entropy on shifted token logits, without comparing negative or candidate documents in embedding space.

question: Why is bidirectional attention used instead of causal masking in embedding models?
pos_doc: Bidirectional attention allows every token in the sequence to attend to all other tokens across past and future positions, creating a unified representation of the entire text rather than predicting the next sequential token with causal left-to-right masks.
neg_doc: Causal masking prevents the model from attending to preceding context, ensuring that embedding vectors only encode the final punctuation token of a document.

question: What is the purpose of in-batch negatives in bi-encoder training?
pos_doc: In-batch negatives treat positive passages from other queries within the same GPU batch as additional negative examples at zero additional forward computation cost, effectively scaling the negative pool to B - 1 passages per query.
neg_doc: In-batch negatives replace the positive document with an adversarial prompt to artificially reduce gradient norms during distributed backpropagation.

question: How does hard negative mining improve retrieval model accuracy?
pos_doc: Hard negative mining samples non-relevant documents that have high lexical or embedding similarity to the query, forcing the model to learn fine-grained semantic boundaries rather than distinguishing obvious, trivial negatives.
neg_doc: Hard negative mining randomly selects unrelated documents from different language corpora to ensure the model memorizes syntax rules.

question: Why is L2 normalization applied to embedding vectors?
pos_doc: Applying L2 normalization scales every embedding vector to unit length, ensuring that cosine similarity between two vectors simplifies directly to an efficient inner dot product and prevents vector magnitude from skewing retrieval scores.
neg_doc: L2 normalization adds Gaussian noise to attention weights to prevent vanishing gradients in deep recurrent layers.

question: What is the difference between mean pooling and last-token pooling?
pos_doc: Mean pooling computes the element-wise average of all non-padded token hidden states in the sequence, capturing balanced semantic signals across the full input, whereas last-token pooling selects only the final hidden state, which is standard in causal generative decoders.
neg_doc: Mean pooling discards all token embeddings except the first token, while last-token pooling averages all hidden states across attention heads.

question: What role does the temperature parameter play in contrastive training?
pos_doc: The temperature parameter scales the dot-product similarity logits before applying the softmax operator; lower temperature values sharpen the probability distribution over hard negatives and penalize close non-relevant candidates more aggressively.
neg_doc: The temperature parameter controls the stochasticity of top-k token decoding during autoregressive text generation.
